Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning
for Object Search in Dynamic Interactive Environments

Kaiyao Liao1,†Qingfeng Li1,†Xinlei Zhang1Chen Chen2Qing Sun2Jianwei Niu1,*

1 School of Computer Science and Engineering, Beihang University2 Zhejiang Key Laboratory of Industrial Big Data and Robot Intelligent Systems, Hangzhou Innovation Institute of Beihang University

† Equal contribution   ·   * Corresponding author

Paper IEEE Xplore ↗Code GitHub ↗Video YouTube ↗

Abstract

Searching for objects in a large, changing home requires more than knowing which room an object belongs to. Robots must understand functional areas, inspect containers, and adapt when objects move. Existing scene graphs often provide coarse spatial divisions, leading to exhaustive exploration and limited use of past experience.

We introduce CMAR-search, a framework for Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning. A Functional 3D Scene Graph (F3DSG) organizes the environment into functional areas and their containers. This structure enables hierarchical planning: reason about an entire area, then optimize the inspection order of its containers. By combining real-time perception, accumulated memory, and commonsense about object use, CMAR-search also supports dynamic object relocalization. Simulation and real-world experiments evaluate search success, efficiency, and adaptation to environmental changes.

Search with context

Know where to look.
Remember what changed.

A kitchen is more than a collection of cabinets. Its functional areas tell a robot where food is likely to be stored or prepared. CMAR uses that commonsense to choose an area, then uses memory to refine the search.

“I'd like to eat some fruit.”

The robot can inspect the preparation area, remember where fruit was seen, and reason about another plausible location when it is no longer there.

CMAR-search in action

From functional areas to individual containers

A structured scene representation connects
commonsense reasoning, perception, and environmental memory.

01

Organize the environment

Identify containers and movable objects, then infer functional areas from their relationships. The F3DSG represents spaces by how people use them.

02

Plan at two scales

An LLM chooses an area-level action. Container inspection is ordered using path distance, semantic relevance, and the risk of skipping a plausible location.

03

Respond to changes

Check the remembered area and original container first. Update the scene graph from new observations, and use commonsense to reason about relocated objects.

Structured context, grounded decisions

The paper's prompt examples show how object relationships
become functional areas and actionable search plans.

Beyond simulation

A real household with an open-layout kitchen and living room,
a separate bedroom, and interactive cabinets and drawers.

Ten episodes per task evaluate Interactive Object Search, Novel Target Search, and Target Relocalization.
Both methods succeed in all real-world trials; CMAR-search uses fewer object interactions and shorter travel distances. Paper Table VI.
